The Parable of the Man in the Well

I bow to the omniscient Lord who carries beings across the ocean of existence, and I briefly describe the condition of worldly souls — which is truly terrifying.

Once a man found himself in a fearsome forest. There he saw a ferocious lion and, terrified, began to run. As he fled, he suddenly fell into a deep well. As he tumbled in, his hands caught hold of the roots of a tree. He clung to them, dangling in mid-air.

On that tree was a beehive. When the lion, pursuing him, jolted the tree, the bees flew away and drops of honey began to drip from the comb — falling directly into the man's mouth. Meanwhile, in the well below, four terrible serpents hissed with open mouths, ready to bite him. And the very roots he clung to were being gnawed by two mice — one black and one white.

In such a dreadful state of suffering, the man made no effort to free himself. Instead, greedy for the taste of those honey drops, he could not resist their allure and began desiring even more. At that moment a Vidyadhar — a celestial being — happened to pass by. Seeing the man's pitiful condition, he was moved to pity and called out, "Brother, come! Sit in my flying chariot. I shall carry you out of here."

The wretched man replied, "Yes, just wait a moment — this drop of honey is falling. Let me have it and then I shall come." The drop fell. The Vidyadhar urged him again, but the man gave the same answer: "Yes, this next drop is coming — I shall be there in a moment." In short, the Vidyadhar reasoned with him many times, but the man remained trapped in the hope of catching the next falling drop. At last, helpless, the poor Vidyadhar had to leave. Truly, beings deluded by sense pleasures never turn their hearts toward their own welfare.

Now understand the meaning of this parable. As the lion chased the man and he fell into the well, so too are living beings driven by the lion of death into the well of worldly existence. The branch of life he clings to is being gnawed day and night by the two mice — the white mouse representing day and the black mouse representing night. The four serpents in the well are the four destinies — human, animal, heavenly, and hellish — waiting to bite him. The drops of honey are the fleeting pleasures of the senses. And the Vidyadhar who offers rescue is the guru, the spiritual teacher who shows the path to liberation.

Yet worldly beings, entranced by the sweet taste of fleeting pleasures, refuse the guru's call. "Just a little more," they think, "just one more enjoyment, and then I shall turn to the spiritual path." But the mice of time gnaw on, the serpents of destiny wait below, and the lion of death draws ever nearer. The honey drops will never cease falling until the branch itself breaks.

This story is the most profound teaching of Jain philosophy: recognize the peril of your condition, heed the guru's call, and do not delay your spiritual awakening for even a single moment. The pleasures of the senses are mere drops of honey — they can never satisfy, and they cost you the priceless opportunity of this human birth.
